groundTruthNarrative: Tri-County Harvest's reported 22% fall in individual donations is mostly not about the new executive director. Of the $520,200 decline, $301,200 is recurring gifts. That drop began at the first automated charge run after the February 2026 database migration, the day before she started: 702 sustainer profiles were imported without payment methods and are never charged. The vendor left the old CardVault schedules running, and $181,300 of unidentified CardVault deposits sits in suspense. These may be sustainer gifts (a recording gap) or corporate pledges and tenant fees, so how much donor money was really lost is unknown. The $70,000 major-gift drop is one deceased donor's one-time 2025 gift; major-donor renewal is stable. The remaining small-donor decline (about 12%) coincides with a local mill closure and with the director's advocacy-focused appeal, and the current evidence cannot separate the two. The board deferred the reconciliation she requested. Evidence is insufficient for a substantive intervention: reconciling CardVault and splitting giving by county are the decisive next steps, and terminating her on the stated grounds would punish the wrong party.

answers.rationale: The largest component of the decline, recurring gifts (-$301,200 of -$520,200, 58%; E2), fell at the automated 2026-03-01 run configured at go-live, the day before the ED started on 2026-03-02 (E3, E5). It fell because fewer charges were attempted (1,108 to 406), not because donors cancelled (decline rate and cancellations flat, E5, E8). The major-gift drop is fully accounted for by the Brandt gift (E9). At most the small-donor decline (-$149,000, 29%) could be attributed to her, so 'primary cause' is counted against by the evidence. The chair's timing claim (E1) does not survive the run log.

Excluding the one-time $75,000 Brandt gift from a donor who died in 2025, major gifts rose from $445,000 (40 donors) to $450,000 (43 donors), and renewal (33/40) matches the prior year (32/39) (E9). Ruth Okafor, the donor quoted by the chair, gave the same $12,000 in 2026 (E10). The ED did not make stewardship calls (E10, E14), but there is no major-gift decline left for that to explain.

Unemployment rose sharply in Ashby County (38% of donors) and pantry need rose 31% (E11), consistent with a downturn. But the small-donor decline (about -12%) is larger than the anonymous, non-regional statewide median of -4% (E12), and the spring appeal letter changed at the same time with no split test or county breakdown (E13). The evidence cannot tell how much of the decline is economic versus messaging or the stewardship vacancy.

GiveLedger stopped charging the 702 pending sustainers (E5, E6), but the vendor left the legacy CardVault schedules running (E6), and $25,100-$26,600 per month of unidentified CV-BATCH deposits continues (E7). That amount is roughly what the corporate pledges plus tenant fees ($25,500/month) would produce, and also roughly what about 420 sustainers at the historical $61 average would produce. If it is corporate and tenant money, nearly all 702 stopped giving. If it is sustainer gifts, only about 280 did. The 31 'my gift stopped' complaints (E8) show some sustainers stopped, but not how many. Without transaction-level data neither reading is favoured. The vendor report does not say how many sustainer schedules were native to CardVault (E6), so the deposits cannot be ruled in or out as sustainer money by arithmetic.

The reported figure comes from donor-database records only and excludes suspense receipts (E2). $181,300 sits in suspense (E7), which is 35% of the $520,200 decline if it is all sustainer money, but it may be almost entirely corporate pledges and tenant fees that historically used the same account (E7). Since the contents cannot be seen, whether more than a quarter of the decline is a recording gap cannot be determined.

The spring appeal response fell from 7.0% to 6.1% after the ED's advocacy rewrite, and 4 complaints mention its political tone (E8, E13). But there was no control letter, the downturn is a simultaneous rival (E11), and the staff survey (E16) has no donor items and no baseline. A contribution is plausible but neither established nor ruled out.

Temporal order runs the wrong way: recurring revenue dropped at the automated 2026-03-01 run, before the 2026-03-02 start date (E3, E5). Revenue then stayed flat at about $25k per month (E5). The mechanism is fewer attempted charges, not cancellations (cancellations 23 vs 27, E8). A different mechanism, the migration's pending profiles, explains the drop (E6).

Temporal order: cutover 2026-02-16, first run 2026-03-01 (E3, E5). Mechanism: 702 profiles imported without a payment method are never charged (E6), and attempted charges fell by exactly 702 (1,108 to 406; E5). Rivals ruled out: per-charge decline rates and donor cancellations were unchanged (E5, E8), and the ED had not started. The edge concerns recorded revenue only. Whether the money is really lost is the separate question H4.

Small-donor giving fell (E2) over the same period in which Ashby unemployment rose 3.8% to 6.4% (E11), so the two co-occur. But the appeal rewrite and the development-director vacancy coincide (E4, E13), and there is no county-level giving split showing that the decline concentrates in Ashby. Causation is not established.

The response rate fell from 7.0% to 6.1% in the year the letter was rewritten (E13), and a few donors objected to its tone (E8). But no split test was run, and the downturn (E11) affects response over the same period. Co-occurrence is established; causation is not.

The 2025 total includes a one-time $75,000 gift from a donor who has since died (E9). Removing it, major gifts are flat to slightly up, and donor count and renewal are stable. The missing gift fully accounts for the -$70,000 by direct accounting decomposition, and the alternative (lost donor relationships) is ruled out by the renewal data.

The stated grounds are counted against by the evidence: 58% of the decline began before her start through a migration defect, and the major-gift drop is a deceased donor's one-time gift (E2, E5, E6, E9). Dismissal on those grounds punishes the wrong party. It costs $62,500 in severance during a revenue shortfall (E17). It would make a second leadership transition within a year while the development post is vacant (E4). It would also remove the one leader who has pressed for the reconciliation that the board deferred (E14, E15). Her contract sets no 2026 fundraising targets, and her formal review is not due until March 2027 (E17).

The largest uncertainty is what the $181,300 of CV-BATCH deposits contains (E7), given that the legacy schedules were never cancelled (E6). This single reconciliation resolves H4 and H5, corrects the board's 22% figure (E2), and determines the right sustainer remedy. It is cheap ($6,500 estimate, E15) and was already proposed (E14).

This action would be right if the pending sustainers' gifts have truly stopped (H4). But the vendor left the CardVault schedules active (E6), and unidentified CardVault deposits continue (E7). Donors who are still being charged there and re-enter their cards could be double-charged. Committing before reconciliation is not justified, though some outreach will probably be needed once the facts are known.

The account is still producing about $25,000 a month of real receipts whose source is unknown (E7). It may be carrying the very sustainer schedules in question (E6). Closing it would stop those payments and, under CardVault's terms, purge the transaction history after 30 days (E7). That destroys the evidence needed to diagnose the decline and possibly cuts off revenue.

The 2025 stewardship calls have had no owner since May (E4, E10, E14), so assigning them is reasonable and low-risk. It is not among the best actions because major-gift giving and renewal are currently stable (E9). The action does not address the recurring-gift question, which dominates the decline, or the uncertainty about the size of the decline. Most 2026 major-donor repeat gifts (21 of 33) arrived after the calls stopped in May (E9).

The size of the real decline is uncertain, because $181,300 of unidentified receipts may or may not be donor money (E2, E7). Whether the pending sustainers are lost or still charged is unknown (E6, E7). The split of the small-donor decline between economy and messaging cannot be resolved without county or segment data (E11, E12, E13). Only evidence-gathering and low-risk holding actions are justified now; a substantive personnel or donor-remediation intervention is not.
